title: The Commercial Production of Ice in the Nineteenth Century

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the summer of 1844, the Wenham Lake Ice Company – named for the lake in the state of Massachusetts, USA, where the ice came from – took premises in a street in central London called the Strand, and there each day placed a fresh block of ice in the window. No one in England had ever seen a block of ice that big before – certainly not in summer, not in the middle of London – or one that was so wondrously glassy and clear. You could actually read a newspaper through it: one was regularly propped behind the block so that passers-by could see this amazing fact for themselves. The shop window became a sensation, and was regularly crowded with spectators.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The eminent English writer Thackeray mentioned Wenham ice in one of his books. Queen Victoria insisted on its use at Buckingham Palace, and made the company her official supplier of ice. Charles Lyell, the English geologist, was so intrigued that he made a special trip to the lake. He was fascinated by how slowly Wenham ice seemed to melt, and assumed it had something to do with its celebrated purity. In fact, Wenham ice melted at the same speed as any other ice. Except that it had travelled far, it wasn't actually special in any way at all.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: But lake ice in general was a marvellous product. It created itself at no cost, was clean, renewable and infinite in supply. The only drawbacks were that there was no infrastructure to collect and store it, and no market to sell it to. In order to make the ice industry exist, it was necessary to work out ways to cut and lift ice on a large scale, build storehouses and engage a reliable chain of shippers and agents. Above all, a demand had to be created in places where ice had seldom or never been seen, and was most assuredly not something anyone was predisposed to pay for. The man who did all this was an American from Boston named Frederic Tudor. Making ice a commercial proposition became his obsession.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Tudor's notion of shipping ice from New England to distant ports was considered completely mad – 'the vagary of a disordered brain', in the words of one of his contemporaries. His first shipment of ice to Britain so puzzled customs officials as to how to classify it, that it melted away before it could be moved off the docks. Ship owners were highly reluctant to accept it as cargo. They didn't relish the humiliation of arriving in a port with a holdful of useless water, but they were also wary of the very real danger of tons of shifting ice and sloshing meltwater making their ships unstable. These were men, after all, whose nautical instincts were based entirely on the idea of keeping water outside the ship.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It cost Frederic Tudor years of frustrated endeavour, and all of his family fortune, to get the ice business launched, but gradually it caught on and eventually it made him rich. For several decades, ice was the USA's second biggest 'crop', measured by weight. If securely insulated, ice could last a surprisingly long while. It could even survive the 16,000-mile, 130-day trip from the east coast of the USA to the west coast of India – or at least about two-thirds of it could, enough to make this long trip profitable. Ice was also sent to the furthest corners of South America, and from New England to California via Cape Horn. Sawdust, a by-product of the timber industry, previously without any value at all, proved to be an excellent insulator, providing useful extra income for Maine lumber mills.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Lake Wenham was actually completely incidental to the ice business in the USA. It never produced more than about ten thousand tons of ice in a year, compared with almost a million tons just from the Kennebec River in Maine. Even in England, Wenham ice was more talked about than used. A few businesses took regular deliveries, but hardly any households (other than the royal one) did. By the 1850s, little of the ice sold in Britain was from the USA. Norway began to refer to Lake Oppegard, near Oslo, as Lake Wenham, so that it could tap into the lucrative market. By the 1850s, most ice sold in Britain was in fact Norwegian, though it has to be said that ice never really caught on with the British. The real market, it turned out, was in the USA itself.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Americans already used ice to chill beverages, to make icy cocktails, to soothe fevers and to create frozen treats such as ice cream. Where ice really came into its own, however, was on the railway, because it allowed the refrigerated transport of perishable food from coast to coast. Chicago became the epicentre of the railway industry in part because it could generate and keep huge quantities of ice. Individual ice houses in Chicago held up to 250,000 tons of ice. Before ice, milk could only be kept for an hour or two in hot weather before it began to spoil, and meat or fish were seldom safe for more than a day.
